intelligence.human_view: Think of a bathroom scale that reads five pounds heavy. You can diet heroically for a month, or you can put a known weight on the scale and fix the scale. Every family in this story chose the known weight — and wrote down what it read before and after, so nobody had to take their word for it.
intelligence.simple_view: Imagine you finally win the big race at school. Winning once is great. But the real magic is writing down your training plan — how you practised, what you ate, the trick for the start — so you can win again next month, and your friends can use the plan too and get faster. A win you can't repeat is luck. A win with a plan is skill. And sharing the plan doesn't make you slower — it makes your whole team faster, and somehow you get faster too.
intelligence.grandma_view: It is how a good sermon or a good letter has always worked: one point, made fully, then the next. The preachers who lost the congregation were never short of material — they had three sermons braided into one and a text you had to squint at. Say the thing once, say it completely, in the order a listener's mind actually walks, and sit down before you start repeating yourself. Brevity is not the goal; completeness without repetition is.
